newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: CANBERRA WATCH-Industry policy is back.
newsitem.headline: CANBERRA WATCH-Industry policy is back.

text.p: Industry policy is set to regain a prominence it has not enjoyed in Australian politics for decades.
The Labor Party, now in opposition, has embraced industry policy as it never did in power.
More importantly, research published last week shows that the community has a powerful desire for industry policy.
The research also shows that the Broken Hill Proprietary Co Ltd's (BHP) decision last month to shut down its steelmaking plant in Newcastle has shaken the country.

"Perhaps no single announcement by a company in recent years has had a greater unsettling impact on ordinary Australians than this one has," social researcher Rod Cameron said in a little-reported speech last week.
Industry policy -- that is, a public strategy to guide business investment -- was only ever held just below the surface by the Labor government in its period of economic rationalism.
Voters find government micro-intervention in the economy intuitively desirable and few believed the economic textbooks that tell them to just let the market make all the decisions.
The push for intervention never stops, and Labor resisted it for years only with the ideological support of the conservative Liberal-National coalition, then in opposition.
The Liberal-Nationals, now in power, are not getting the same support from Labor which, in its hasty shift to the Left since the 1996 election, has embraced industry intervention.
Labor members feel genuinely comfortable pushing for an industry policy. It is a good populist policy, too: all the upsides are easily understood while the downside is murky economic theory.
Moreover, the appalling fact that unemployment has stopped falling at around 8.5 percent must be good evidence to many voters that economic rationalism and a free market has produced no solution.
Cameron said the government had magnified the effect of BHP's decision to close Newcastle steelmaking when it said the decision was unavoidable.
"What kind of answer is that?" the average person must have wondered. "Three thousand jobs go out the door and the government says nothing can be done?"

Cameron's ANOP Research Services Pty Ltd picked up such attitudes in the process of conducting research in Melbourne and Sydney for the mining industry, and he delivered the results in a speech to the Minerals Council national convention on May 29.

"What I am confident of concluding from the preliminary study of attitudes in our nation's two biggest cities is that aspects of industry policy will dominate political debate in the years immediately ahead," he said.
In short, these are the factors that Cameron found were driving the national attention towards industry policy:
--Seemingly intractable unemployment and fears of job security.
--BHP's planned shutdown at Newcastle.
--The absence of jobs for apprentices finishing their training, evidence of a decline in manufacturing.
--Nostalgia for a time when Australia made things and the current reliance on imports is combining with a consensus that tariff cuts have gone far enough.
--"Toss in headlines about the balance of payments and you have quite considerable concern about the growing absence of Australian-made goods and produce."

The government will certainly respond. Whatever Prime Minister John Howard's inclinations towards dry economics, he will feel great pressure to implement some kind of industry policy as Labor campaigns for one.
The alternative would be to lose votes.
